procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Sessions Judge at Bidar
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 18th June, 1953 of the High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad in Confirmation Case No. 376/6 of 1952-53 and Criminal Appeals Nos. 394/6, 395/6 and 392/6 of 1952-53
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge at Bidar issued a Judgment and Order dated 2nd June, 1952 in Sessions Case No. 9/8 of 1951-52. Five convicts from that case applied to the High Court for leave to appeal. The High Court heard the petition (presumably denying leave to appeal, though this is not explicitly stated).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The convicts (Pandurang, Tukia, and Bhillia) appealed to the Supreme Court by Special Leave, which was granted on January 18, 1954.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Ordinance came within Head 27 of List 2 of the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act, concerning 'Trade and commerce within the Province; markets and fair; money lending and money lenders', and whether the Provincial Legislature was competent to legislate on that topic.

law.name: Head 27 of List 2 of the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act
law.description: This provision grants a Provincial Legislature the power to legislate on matters concerning 'Trade and commerce within the Province; markets and fair; money lending and money lenders'.

reasoning.conclusion: The Court concluded that the Ordinance fell within the scope of Head 27 of List 2 of the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act, and therefore, the Provincial Legislature was competent to enact it.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Ordinance came within Head 27 of List 2 of the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act, concerning 'Trade and commerce within the Province; markets and fair; money lending and money lenders', and whether the Provincial Legislature was competent to legislate on that topic.
appellant_arguments: The Ordinance came within Head 27 of List 2 of the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act:-"Trade and commerce within the Province; markets and fair; money lending ahd money lenders'', and that the Provincial Legislature was competent to legislate on that topic.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The inference of common intention must be a necessary inference deduced from the circumstances of the case. It can be proven either by direct proof of prior concert or by circumstantial evidence where the incriminating facts are incompatible with the innocence of the accused and incapable of explanation on any other reasonable hypothesis. The determination of common intention is a question of fact in every case, and the facts of one case cannot be used as a precedent to determine the conclusion on the facts in another.
obiter: When appellate judges agree on the question of guilt but differ on the question of sentence, it is usual not to impose the death penalty unless there are compelling reasons.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the Ordinance came within Head 27 of List 2 of the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act, which concerns 'Trade and commerce within the Province; markets and fair; money lending and money lenders', and consequently, the Provincial Legislature was competent to legislate on that topic.
